prompt: On a graphing app you zoom in on $f(x) = x^2$ at the point $x = 3$ until the curve looks like a straight line. The average rates of change from $x = 3$ to $x = 3.1$, then to $3.01$, then to $3.001$ come out as $6.1$, $6.01$, and $6.001$. What number are those rates heading toward?
hint: Read the list like a limit: where are $6.1, 6.01, 6.001$ going?

hints.text: Read the list like a limit: where are $6.1, 6.01, 6.001$ going?

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Do the same squeeze at $x = 1$ on $f(x) = x^2$. From $1$ to $1.1$ the rate is $\frac{1.21 - 1}{0.1} = 2.1$; from $1$ to $1.01$ it is $2.01$. Those head to $2$. Notice $2$ is double the $x$-value. Now read your own list the same way.
Each time the second point moves ten times closer, the rate gets ten times closer to a single number.
The rates squeeze down to $6$ — the INSTANT rate of change at $x = 3$.

explanation: The average rate between two points is the slope of the line joining them.
As the second point slides toward $x = 3$, the extra bit shrinks: $6.1 \to 6.01 \to 6.001$.
The leftovers $0.1, 0.01, 0.001$ are being squeezed to nothing.
The limit is $6$: the slope of the curve at that exact instant.

alternativeExplanations.title: Do the algebra once
steps: Take a step of size h: the rate is ((3 + h)² − 9) ÷ h.
Expand the top: 9 + 6h + h² − 9 = 6h + h². Divide by h to get 6 + h.
Now let h shrink to 0 and the answer is plainly 6 — the h was the whole "extra bit" in 6.1 and 6.01.

alternativeExplanations.title: Keep zooming on the map
steps: Zooming into a curve is like zooming into a map of a curved coastline.
Zoom far enough and any smooth curve stops looking curved and looks like one straight street.
The slope of that street is the instant rate: 6. That is the exact idea calculus is built on.
